translations.text: The Fourth Book, concerning the Maccabees and Their Mother.
I am preparing to present a philosophical discourse before you: whether sound reason, obedient to the fear of God, has sovereign power. I sincerely advise you to examine this philosophy diligently.
For it is necessary and useful to everyone, especially to those who desire virtue, since it sustains disciplined reason.
If virtuous reason is seen to rule over the passions that disturb self-control—over debauchery and desire—

and not only over these, but is also seen to have power over other passions that obstruct righteousness, over evil habits, and over other passions that hinder courage: over anger, over giving way before afflictions, and over fear.
Perhaps someone will say, “If the mind has power over the passions, why does it not have power over forgetfulness [?] and ignorance?” But in saying this, they make an argument worthy of ridicule.

For it does not have power over its own passions, but over the passions that oppose courage, righteousness, and self-control. Its power over these does not mean that it can abolish them, but that it need not be overcome by them.
I can show from many other examples that reason obedient to the fear of God rules over the passions.
But I demonstrate this especially from the steadfastness of those who died for the fear of God. I mean Eleazar, the seven brothers, and their mother.
For all these endured pains that brought them to death and showed that reason has power over the passions.
Among praiseworthy people, it is these whom I now intend to celebrate: those who died at that time for the fear of God, together with their mother. I pronounce them blessed for their sufferings.

For their courage made them an object of wonder not only to all other people, but even to those who tortured them. They brought about the downfall of the tyranny over the people, defeated the tyrant, and purified their country.

It will now be easy for us to speak about this after explaining the subject of our discourse, as we are accustomed to do. Then, with the help of God, who makes everyone wise, we will turn our discourse to these matters.
Our inquiry, then, is this: whether reason has authority over passion.
Let us examine what reason is, what passion is, how many kinds of passion there are, and whether reason has power over them all.
Reason, then, is the mind that rightly chooses a life of wisdom.
Wisdom is knowledge of divine and human matters and of their causes.
This, then, is instruction in the law, through which we learn about divine matters in an exalted way and about human matters in a fitting way.
The parts of wisdom are these: sound judgment, justice, and self-control.
The foremost of them all is prudence, through which reason rules over all our passions.
The basic kinds of passion, within which the others are included, are two: pleasure and distress. These accompany the soul.
Many passions are arranged in succession after them.
Desire comes before pleasure, and joy follows it.
Fear comes before distress, and sorrow follows distress.
Anger is a passion shared by pleasure and distress. A person recognizes that this is so when he falls into it.
Within pleasure, then, there is an inclination toward evil passions, whose forms are more numerous than those of all the other passions.
For it produces these things in the soul: arrogance, love of money, love of praise, and contentiousness.
In the body, however, eating anything, overcoming one's stomach, and eating [?].
Just as these two—pleasure and distress, which arise from pains—are plants belonging to both body and soul, so the branches of these passions are numerous.
Reason obedient to the fear of God cultivates each one of them, clears it, prunes it, grafts it, fences it in, and waters it, and clears away [?] all the growths that produce pain.
For the mind is the guide of virtue and the ruler over the passions. Its power over the passions is seen first through actions that disturb self-control.
A person's self-control, then, consists in overcoming desires.
Some of these belong to the soul and some to the body. It is evident that it has power over both kinds.
Otherwise, when we are moved to eat something forbidden, how do we turn ourselves away from our desires? Is it not because reason can overcome desires? That is what I think.
For we desire to eat creatures of the sea, birds, four-footed animals, and all kinds of food, but we restrain ourselves because of reason’s authority.
We obey, and the passions of desire are brought under control, restrained by disciplined reason; all the impulses of the body are bridled.
Nor is it surprising if the soul's desires, which long for beauty, are restrained.
For Joseph is praised in this way: through sound judgment he overcame the pleasure of passion.
For when he is young and at that vigorous age when a person becomes capable of sexual intercourse, the wildness of his passions is quieted within him.
Reason is shown to be capable of overcoming not only licentious conduct itself, but also every kind of desire.
For the law says, “Do not desire your neighbor's wife, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”
Indeed, even if the law had not said, “You shall not covet,” I could still convince you that reason can overcome desires, just as it can overcome actions that obstruct righteousness.

Otherwise, how does someone who is a glutton or a drunkard learn proper conduct and abandon his former habits, unless it is clear that reason obedient to the fear of God has authority over the passions?

For as soon as he begins to live according to the law, even if he loves money, he compels himself to lend to the needy. He lends his money without interest, keeps track of the sabbatical periods, and forgives what is owed to him.

Even if he is miserly, he is overcome by the law through virtuous reason: he does not gather the scattered grain at harvest or strip his vineyard bare. From his conduct it is easy to recognize that reason has authority over the passions.
For the law also has authority over the love of children for their parents, so that they do not deny them and fulfill what the law requires.
It also has authority over marital love: if she acts unlawfully, he kills her.

It also has authority over the love of parents for their children, and through their parents it brings punishment upon them for their wickedness. It also has authority over the affection of friends, rebuking them for their wickedness through their friends.
Do not suppose that what I have said is something novel, since reason can even overcome hostility because of the law.
He does not cut down his enemies’ fine trees, but preserves them so that they remain his enemies’ property, and he raises up those that have fallen.
Reason is also shown to overcome violent passions: the love of power, the love of praise, boastfulness, arrogance, and envy.
For the person who lives with self-control restrains and subdues all these hateful passions, just as he also overcomes anger. For reason has authority over this too.
When Moses became angry with Dathan and Abiram, he did not act against them in anger. Instead, through the gentleness of his reason, he restrained his anger as though by a judicial ruling.
For, as I have said, reason can gain victory over the passions, holding some in check and weakening others.

Otherwise, why did our father Jacob, wise in everything, rebuke Simeon and Levi because they had acted without reason and killed the inhabitants of Shechem, the entire population without exception? He said, “Cursed are their anger and their wrath, because it is cruel.”
For if reason could not overcome anger, he would not have spoken this way.
For when God created the human being, he planted passions and impulses within him.
But through the senses he made holy reason king over them all and seated it as though on a throne.
He gave him this law so that, by conducting himself according to it, he might exercise a gentle, just, and courageous rule.
How, then, can you say, “Does reason rule over all the passions?”
For this statement is quite ridiculous. The mind is not shown to have authority over its own passions, but over bodily passions. How is this so?
It is impossible for any of you to feel no desire, but the law can keep a person from being enslaved to his desire.
No one can cut anger out of his soul, but reason can help him not to become angry.
A person cannot rid himself of the bitterness of his impulses, but reason can help him not to be overcome by it.
For reason does not uproot the passions; rather, it opposes them.
We can understand this clearly through King David’s thirst.
For he had fought the Philistines all day and had slaughtered many of them, together with the soldiers from the people who were with him.
Evening had now overtaken him, and, sweating heavily and exhausted, he was hurrying to reach his royal tent. Around it, on either side, the army of our ancestors was encamped.
While everyone was occupied with the evening meal,
The king was very thirsty, although springs were readily available to him in abundance, and he could have relieved his thirst with them.
But an irrational desire tormented him to drink water from enemy territory, and this made him restless and inflamed him.

Some of his soldiers sighed and lamented over his desire. Two young soldiers, strong and courageous men, were stirred by the king’s desire. They took a jug, put on all their armor, and crossed their enemies’ borders and the outposts of their men lying in ambush.
They concealed themselves from the gatekeepers and went out searching among the enemy,
looking for where the water was. They courageously brought the king a drink from it.
But although he was burning fiercely with thirst, he considered it a harsh and dangerous thing, judging that the drink was being weighed against blood.
For this reason he set good judgment against his desire and poured out to God the drink that had been brought to him.
For virtuous reason can overcome the compelling force of the passions and soften the coarseness of licentiousness.
It can also withstand the sufferings of the body and, through love of what is good, disdain all the compelling forces of the passions.
But now the time calls us to recount the story of virtuous reason.

For the law brought profound peace to our fathers, and they enjoyed prosperity and ease. Even King Seleucus Nicator set aside gold and silver for their service in the sanctuary, and their way of life was acceptable to him.
Then certain people, through their disruptive behavior, disturbed the harmony of the community, and they fell into troubles of various kinds.

For a certain Simon opposed the conduct of Onias, who then held the high priesthood, a good and noble man. After slandering him before the people in every possible way without succeeding in harming him, Simon fled and went away to betray his country.
For this purpose he came to Apollonius, who held authority over Syria, Phoenicia, and Cilicia.

He said to him, “As someone devoted to the king’s interests, I have come to inform you that vast sums of silver belonging to people who perform no service there are deposited with the priests in the treasury at Jerusalem. These rightfully belong to King Seleucus.”
When Apollonius heard this, he praised Simon for his boldness on the king’s behalf. He then went up to King Seleucus and informed him about these deposits of silver.
He received authority over the matter and quickly entered our country with the accursed Simon and a powerful army.
He said that he had come in obedience to the king’s commands, to take from the treasury the silver belonging to [?].
The people were appalled at his words and argued against him. They considered it a bitter thing if those who had trusted the sanctuary’s treasury were to be defrauded of their deposits.
Apollonius proceeded toward the temple with threats.
The elders, together with women and children, pleaded with God to stretch his protecting hand over the holy place that was being treated with contempt.
But when Apollonius went up with a force of armed men to plunder that silver, mounted angels appeared to him from heaven, their weapons flashing. They filled him with great fear and trembling.

Apollonius even fell to the ground in the temple and was close to death. He raised his hands to heaven and, with many tears, begged the Hebrews to pray for him and appease the heavenly powers that had come against him.
For he said that he deserved to die because he had sinned, but that if he survived, he would tell everyone about the blessedness of the temple.
Onias the high priest was persuaded by these words. He also feared that King Seleucus might think Apollonius had been killed through a human plot rather than by divine judgment, so he prayed for him.
And so he miraculously survived and departed to tell the king what had happened to him.
When King Seleucus died, his son Antiochus, called Epiphanes, succeeded to his rule—a deceitful and wicked man.
He removed Onias from the high priesthood and appointed his brother Jason high priest on a condition:
If he granted him the office, Jason would pay him an annual tribute of three thousand six hundred and sixty talents.
He permitted him to become high priest and gave him authority to govern the people.
This man changed the people’s way of life and their laws, leading them into every kind of lawbreaking.
He not only established a gymnasium in the capital of our whole country, but also put an end to concern for the temple.
Because of these things, God's judgment grew severe, and he stirred up Antiochus himself against them.

For while he was fighting Ptolemy in Egypt, he heard that a report of his death had spread and that this had caused great joy among the inhabitants of Jerusalem. He quickly prepared his chariots against them.
After plundering them, he issued a decree that anyone among them found living according to the laws of his ancestors should die.
Yet he could find no way through his decrees to destroy the people’s laws, and he saw that all his threats and tortures were being rendered ineffective.
Even women who circumcised their children were thrown down from high places together with their infants, although they had known beforehand that this would happen to them.
Through torture he tried to force everyone among the people to renounce Judaism by eating defiled food.

Then the tyrant Antiochus sat with his officials on a raised platform, with his troops surrounding him on either side, dressed in their armor. He ordered the spearmen to bring each of the Hebrews forward and force them to eat pork and meat from sacrifices.
If any refused to eat the unclean food, they were to die under the punishment of [?].

As many were being seized in this way, one of the Hebrew people was brought forward first. His name was Eleazar, and he came from a priestly family. He was a scribe versed in the law and was advanced in years. Because of his old age, he was also known to many of the tyrant’s associates. They brought this man before the tyrant.
When the tyrant Antiochus saw him, he said:

“Old man, before I begin torturing you, I give you this advice: eat pork and live. For I have respect for your years and these white hairs of yours. After all this time, you do not seem to me to be acting wisely by following the Jewish religion.
For why, when nature has provided the flesh of this animal as excellent food, do you shrink from it and reject it?
It is foolish not to enjoy pleasures that involve no disgrace, and it is wrong to reject what nature offers and gives.
But you appear even more foolish than this if, pursuing a love of glory for the sake of truth,
you also despise me and scorn punishment. Will you not wake up from the foolishness of this teaching,
shake off this senseless notion, adopt a way of thinking suited to your years and your old age, and learn the truth about what is beneficial?
“Bow to the kindness of my mercy and have pity on your old age.
For you must also consider that, even if there is some being who watches over your religion, he will forgive you every violation of the laws that you commit under compulsion.”
While the tyrant was urging him in this way to eat meat that the law did not permit, Eleazar asked for permission to speak.
When he received permission to speak, he began to address the whole assembly as follows:
“Antiochus, since we are convinced that we should live according to the law, no compulsion is stronger for us than obedience to the law.
“For this reason, we are determined not to transgress it in any way.
Even if our law were not truly divine, as you firmly believe, but we nevertheless believed it to be divine [?], even then we would not be permitted to abandon our conviction about reverence for God.
“Do not suppose, then, that it is a small sin for us to eat defiled food.
“For transgressing the law in small matters or in great ones has the same force.
“In either case, it is equally an act of arrogance against the law.
“You mock our teaching, as though we did not follow it with sound judgment.
It teaches self-control, so that we may overcome every desire and passion, and train ourselves in courage, so that we may willingly endure every affliction.
It teaches the justice inherent in our nature, so that we may obey the law in every way. It also teaches true reverence for God, so that we may worship in purity the one who alone is God.
For this reason we eat nothing defiling. Because we believe that the law comes from God, we are convinced that the Maker of the world accommodates his commands to the weakness of our nature.
He has therefore permitted us to eat those things that are not harmful to our lives, but has forbidden us to eat the flesh of those that are harmful.
It is therefore insolent not only to force us to transgress the law, but also to make us eat, so that you may mock us through this food, which is the most defiling of all.
But do not mock me.
I will not [?] their sacred covenant and the oaths that our fathers swore to keep the law.
Not even if you gouge out my eyes and melt my internal organs.
I am not so old, nor so lacking in courage, that I cannot cultivate and renew my thoughts for the sake of reverence for God.
So prepare the wheels for these things, and stoke the fire fiercely.
I do not cherish my old age so much that I would break the law of my fathers to save my life.
I will not betray you, law, my guide, nor will I deny you, my beloved self-restraint.
I will not put you to shame, O teaching that instructs us in excellence, nor will I renounce you, honored priesthood and instruction in the law.
My old age will not defile my lips, nor will I stain the years in which I have grown old in obedience to the law.
My ancestors will receive me in purity, because I have not shrunk from your acts of coercion, which lead to death.
You use force because you act wickedly, but neither with your own hands nor through your servants can you gain control over my thoughts concerning reverence for God.”
When he had spoken like an orator in this way against the tyrant’s persuasion, the spearmen approached him and cruelly dragged Eleazar away to be tortured.
First they stripped the old man, who was adorned with the outward signs of reverence for God.
Then they twisted his hands behind his back and flogged him with a whip.
One of the tyrant’s soldiers, who had obeyed the king’s commands, was shouting at him in a loud voice.
But Eleazar, truly brave and courageous, was like someone being scourged in a dream. He did not change his resolve in any way.
But while he kept his eyes raised upward, the old man's flesh was torn apart by the lashes, and his blood ran over him as they slashed his sides.
He fell to the ground because his body could not bear the pain. But his mind remained steadfast and did not turn this way or that.
One of those cruel men who were torturing him kicked him in the stomach and struck him to make him get up whenever he fell.
But he endured the pain and scorned their violence. He bore the tortures and despised the tyrant.
Like a determined athlete, the old man defeated his torturers even as he suffered their blows.
As his face grew sweaty and he panted heavily, they marveled at the courage of his soul.
Even those who were torturing him marveled. Because of this, sometimes out of pity for his old age,
sometimes out of sympathy for him, and sometimes out of admiration for his endurance, some of the king's associates approached him and said to him:
“Eleazar, you are destroying yourself through these senseless sufferings.
"We will set some cooked food before you. Pretend that you are eating pork, and live."
But Eleazar, as though this advice they had given him had plunged him into another torment more bitter than the first, cried out in a loud voice:
"Never do the children of Abraham fall into such deceitful thinking that, in pursuit of life, we should dishonestly do something unseemly by assuming a different identity.
For it would also be senseless for us, after living a life of truth right up to the point of death, to change now,
and ourselves become an evil example of ungodliness to the young, giving them a model of eating unclean food.
Then we would live dishonorable lives, becoming a laughingstock to the world because of our degradation.
Should we be despised by the tyrant as weaklings, instead of fighting to the death for our divine law?
For these reasons I tell you, children of Abraham: die courageously for the truth!
And you, servants of the tyrant, why do you delay bringing suffering upon us?"
When they saw that he was so courageous and would not change, they no longer showed him the compassion they had shown before, but brought him to the fire.
There they burned him with cunningly fashioned instruments and poured foul liquid into his nostrils.
When he was burning down to his bones and his soul was about to depart, he raised his eyes to heaven and said:
"You know, God, that I could escape, for I am dying in fiery torment for the sake of the law."
Be reconciled to your people, and let our punishment on their behalf be enough for you.
Make my blood a means of purification for them, and take my life in exchange for theirs.”
After saying these things, this devout man died triumphantly amid the tortures. Even through his death agonies, he remained firm in his resolve for the sake of the law.
It is therefore clear that reason grounded in the fear of God rules over the passions.
For if the passions ruled over reason, I would have testified that the victory was theirs.
But as it is, we rightly attribute to reason authority over the passions, with [?].
We must acknowledge that reason holds control, since it rules even over the sufferings that press upon us from outside.
It is therefore ridiculous for anyone to say that reason does not rule, when we have shown that it conquers not only the passions but also other assaults, without allowing them to overpower it.
For, like a skilled helmsman, the reason of our father, the aged Eleazar, steered his thoughts with the sails of reverence for God through the great sea of tortures and sufferings.
And when the tyrant's assaults and tortures pressed upon him, along with the turbulent waves of affliction,
they did not turn his sails away from reverence for God in any way, until he sailed on and reached the harbor of immortal victory.

Never did a besieged city stand so firmly against many different weapons of war as this man in his full armor. For although his holy soul suffered tortures, afflictions, and burning, he overcame the afflictions surrounding him because his reason was fighting for the truth.
For our father Eleazar raised his reason and lifted it like a towering crag, and he scorned the raging waves of suffering.
O priest worthy of the priesthood! You did not defile your clean lips and teeth, or your stomach, where purity and the fear of God dwelt, by mingling with impure food.
O you who fulfilled the law and taught a godly life!
This is how teachers of the law ought to be: with their blood, their sweat, and their courage, they should struggle through sufferings even to death.

You, our father, gloriously upheld our noble law through your endurance. You praised its holiness and exalted it rather than overthrowing it. Through your deeds you made the words of divine wisdom credible.
O old man, whose resolve was tougher than all tortures! O elder, who proved stronger than fire! Eleazar, great king over the passions!
For just as our father Aaron, armed with his censer as though with a weapon, ran among the people and overcame the burning angel.
so too Eleazar, Aaron’s descendant, did not change his resolve even as he burned in the fire.
But most wonderful of all was this: although he was old, the strength of his limbs was failing, his body was feeble, and his arteries were exhausted, he became young in the spirit of his mind.
And he overcame tortures of many kinds.
O blessed old age, pure conduct, and life lived according to the law! The sure seal of death brought you to perfection.
Therefore, if an old man endured tortures even to death for the sake of truth, it is clear that reason filled with the fear of God rules over the passions.
Perhaps someone will say that not everyone has conquered the passions, since not everyone possesses wise reason.
But those who are devoted to the fear of God are the only ones who can overcome the passions of the body.
Therefore, this does not discredit the argument at all, if some people are seen succumbing to the passions because their reason is weak.
Otherwise, who walks the entire straight path of righteousness and trusts in God,
And it is acknowledged that a person is blessed for virtue if he endures every hardship and does not succumb to the passions for the sake of truth.
For only someone who is wise and courageous has mastery over his passions.
For this reason, the young men too, because their reason was governed by the fear of God, overcame tortures more severe than these.
For in the first trial the tyrant was decisively defeated before everyone's eyes, and he could not compel the old man to eat defiled food.

Then, fiercely, as though driven by passion, he ordered others of the Hebrew people to be brought. If they ate unclean food, they were to be released once they had eaten; but if they refused to comply, they were to be tortured bitterly.
When the tyrant gave these orders, seven young men were brought, dragged along with their elderly mother. They were handsome, modest, and strong, and cheerful in every way.

When the tyrant saw them surrounding their mother like a troop, with her in their midst, he was delighted and marveled at their appearance and their harmony. He gave them a cheerful look, called them to his side, and said:

“Young men, because I sincerely admire the beauty of each one of you and respect this whole company of brothers, I not only advise you not to commit the folly committed by that old man who underwent torture,
but I also ask you to obey me and become my friends. For just as I can punish those who disobey my command, so I can bestow benefits on those who obey me.
Be assured, then, that you will receive authority and high offices in my dominion if you renounce the laws and practices of your ancestors
and adopt pagan practices. For once you change your customs, you will enjoy a life of luxury in your youth.
But if instead you kindle anger in me through your disobedience, you will force me to destroy each one of you with severe tortures.
Therefore, have pity on yourselves. Even I, who am fighting against you, have pity on your lives and compassion for your fine stature and beauty.”
Do not think, then, that anything else will happen to you if you refuse to obey, except that you will die under torture.
After saying this, he ordered the instruments of torture to be arranged before them. He did this because he hoped to persuade them through fear to eat something unclean.

When they brought out the wheels, the iron implements, the joint-dislocators, the stretching straps, the cauldrons, the frying pans, the spits, the iron hands, the wedges, and the burning coals, the tyrant spoke and said:
“Young men, be afraid! Even the Judge whom you fear will forgive you, because you are breaking the law under compulsion.”

But when they heard these words of persuasion and threats, and saw that terrifying sight, they were not alarmed. Instead, they answered the tyrant with wise words, and through their wise reasoning they overthrew his tyranny.
Let us consider what words they would have used in their thoughts if their souls had been fearful and they had lacked courage. Would they not have spoken like this?
“We are miserable and very foolish people. The king is making a request of us and inviting us to enjoy good things. We ought to comply with his wishes.
Why are we acting foolishly and daring to persist in disobedience that brings death?
“Let us fear the tortures, brothers! Let us take their threats to heart, and abandon this love of glory and this pride that brings death.
Let us spare our bodies and feel concern for our mother's old age.
Let us recognize that unless we comply, we will die.
Nor will the divine Judge be angry with us, since we fear the king because of his coercion.
Why are we taking our own life away from this pleasant existence and depriving it of this sweet world?
Let us not drag it by force into distress, nor seek glory through torture.
Even the law itself does not put us to death against our will.
“Where does all this stubbornness rooted in us come from, and this persistence in pretension that brings death, when we could easily obey the king without trouble and live?”
But the young men said none of these things as they were about to undergo suffering, nor did they even entertain such thoughts.
For they scorned suffering and triumphed over pain.
Thus, as soon as the tyrant stopped urging them to eat unclean food, they all spoke together, as though with one voice and one soul:
“Why are you delaying, tyrant? We are ready to die rather than transgress the commandment of our fathers.
“For we would rightly feel ashamed before them if we did not obey the law and take Moses as our counselor.
Tyrant, counselor of lawbreaking, do not pity us for your own sake while you hate us.
“For we consider your mercy toward us, offered in exchange for a life outside the law, harsher than death.
“You try to frighten us by threatening us with death through torture, as though you had not learned a little while ago from Eleazar how weak the power of your tortures is.
“But if an old man, one of humankind, endured suffering and died for the truth, should not we, who are young, endure all the more, despising your cruel tortures, which even our aged teacher overcame?
“Put our souls to the test, then, tyrant! Even if you kill us for the truth, do not think that you defeat us through your tortures.
“For through these sufferings and this endurance we receive the crowns of our victory.”
But you, because you are occupied with killing us, will suffer eternal torment by the judgment of God.
When they said these things, the tyrant became furious with them, not merely as people who refused to obey, but also as opponents who challenged him.
For this reason, the attendants were ordered to bring the eldest of them into the middle. They tore his tunic and bound his hands and arms with a strap on either side.
When they grew weary of flogging him without accomplishing anything, they threw him onto the wheel.
And on the rack the victorious young man was being torn apart at his joints.
While all his limbs were being broken, he spoke out defiantly, saying:

“You unclean tyrant, enemy of heavenly justice, and corrupt in your thinking! You are not torturing me like this because I killed someone, nor because I sinned against God, but because I stand firm for the divine law.”
The attendants were saying to him, “Admit that you will eat, so that you may escape the tortures.”
He said, “Your wheel is not strong enough to subdue my resolve, you unclean attendants! Cut off my limbs and burn my flesh with fire.
“Tear my joints apart! For through every torture I will convince you that the Hebrews alone are invincible in the struggle for virtue.”
While he was saying these things, they lowered the fire beneath him and skillfully tightened the wheels upon him with force.
The wheel was twisting in every direction, and the bed of coals beneath him was being extinguished by the drops of his blood. And as his flesh was melting on the axles of this device:
and his bones were being pulled apart, the courageous young man, a son of Abraham, did not groan.
But, as though he were being transformed in the fire into an imperishable being, he bravely endured the tortures, saying:
“Follow my example, my brothers, and never depart from the company to which I belong. Do not disown your kinship with my courageous spirit. Fight a glorious and victorious fight for the truth,

so that through it the righteous providence of God, which has watched over us since the days of our fathers, may be reconciled to our people and bring punishment upon the head of this tyrant, who is a destructive demon.”
When the noble young man had said these things, he breathed his last.

While everyone was marveling at his endurance, the soldiers dragged forward the one who was next after the first, a young man in stature. They fitted iron hands onto their own hands and, as he hung suspended, threatened to rake him with their sharp claws.
When they asked him whether he wanted to eat before undergoing torture, and heard a courageous answer from him,

they drove the iron hands into the back of his neck and tore away all his flesh up to his chin. Those leopard-like beasts also stripped the skin from his head in this way. But, enduring this suffering nobly, he said:
“How welcome is every form of death for the sake of the faith of our fathers!” He also said to the tyrant:
“Do you not realize, tyrant, most wicked of all tyrants, that you are in far greater distress than I am? For you see that your proud and arrogant purpose has been defeated by endurance for the truth.
“My sufferings are made light for me by my longing for victory.
You are being scourged by the blows of the torments for which your unbelief is reserved. You will not escape the righteous judgment of God, impure tyrant.”
When this man too had endured a death worthy of being recounted forever, they brought forward the third, repeatedly urging him to eat and live.
But he said in a loud voice, “Do you not know that the father who fathered those who died also fathered me? The very same mother gave birth to me too, and I was brought up in the very same teaching.”
I will not deny the glorious faithfulness of my brothers.”
They bitterly resented his boldness, and with instruments for dislocating joints they stretched out and dislocated his hands and feet.
They twisted and cut off his fingers, and broke his arms, his kneecaps, and his elbows.
When they could not overcome him by any means, they released the instruments in which he lay and immediately brought him onto the wheel.
On it his vertebrae were pulled apart and his limbs were dislocated. He watched his flesh splitting open and drops of blood flowing from within him.
When he was close to death, he said:
“We endure these things, you impure tyrant, for the sake of God’s teaching and truth.
“But you, because of your wickedness and your filthy murders, are destined to endure torments that never end.”
When this man too had died as it was fitting for him to die, they dragged forward the fourth, the brother of those who had gone before, saying to him:
“Do not fall into the same madness as your brothers.”
But he said to them, “You have no fire so much hotter than the earlier fire used on my brothers that you can make me recoil.
No—by my brothers’ death, full of blessedness, by the tyrant’s everlasting destruction, and by the unending life of the faithful—I will not disown my noble brotherhood with my brothers.
So use your ingenuity, tyrant, to seek out new tortures, so that through them too you may learn that I am the brother of those who endured your tortures.”
When Antiochus, that blood-licker, thirsty for slaughter and foulest of the foul, heard these things, he ordered them to cut out his tongue.
He said, “Even if you cut out the instrument of my voice, God hears even someone who is silent.
Here is my tongue, hanging out for you. Cut it off! By doing this you will not also cut out the tongue of our thoughts.
We gladly give the chief members of our bodies over to destruction for God’s sake.
“But God will soon take vengeance on you, for you are cutting out a tongue that used to sing divine songs.”
When this one too had endured torture and died, the fifth sprang into the middle and said:
“I do not hesitate, tyrant, to face afflictions for the truth.
“I have stepped forward of my own free will, so that, by tormenting me too, you may receive punishment for your many sins at the heavenly judgment.
You who hate virtue and hate human hearts, what have we done that you destroy us in this way?”
Is it because we worship the Creator and live according to his glorious law?
But this deserved honor, not torture.”
While he was saying these things, the soldiers bound him and brought him to the wooden frame.
On this wooden frame his whole body was bent backward from his neck like a scorpion, and his limbs were being dislocated.
While his spirit was being distressed by this form of torture and his body was being forcibly stretched apart, he said:
You grant us fine favors against your will, tyrant: through severe pains you immerse us in an ordeal that lets us show our endurance for the sake of the Law.
When this one too had died, they brought forward the sixth boy after him. When the tyrant asked whether he was willing to eat and be released, he answered him:
“I am younger than my brothers in years, but in sound judgment I am their equal.
“Since, then, we were born and brought up in these very same things, it is right that we should also die together for their sake.”
If, then, it seems right to you to torture me, I will suffer torture rather than eat what defiles.
When he had said these things, they brought him onto the wheel.
As he was stretched out on it, his limbs and joints were pulled apart, and a fire was kindled beneath him.
They heated sharp spits and drove them into his back. They skewered his ribs and burned his internal organs.
While he was in this agony, he said, “Oh, this glorious contest, to which all of us brothers have been called for the truth, to struggle through these pains without being defeated!
“For whoever is trained in the teaching of truth cannot be defeated, tyrant,
“and is armed with the love of good things. I too will die with my brothers,
I too—I too—am bringing great destruction upon you, you destructive demon, inventor of new tortures and enemy of true worshipers!
“Six young men have overthrown your tyranny.
For the fact that you could not persuade our minds—is that not your humiliation?
“Your fire is cold to us, your iron instruments cause no pain, and your violence has no strength.
For it is not the spear-bearers of tyranny who surround us, but the spear-bearers of the divine Law. That is why our resolve cannot be defeated.”
When this one too had died a blessed death after falling into the cauldron, the seventh came forward. He was the youngest of them all.
The tyrant appeared to grieve for this one out of compassion, although he had been deeply stung by his brothers.
When he saw that the boy was now bound in chains, he sent for him, brought him closer to himself from where he had been standing, and said to him:

“You see the outcome of your brothers’ foolishness. Because of their disobedience, they received punishment and died. If you too refuse to obey, you miserable boy, you will face torments and die from them before your time.”
“But if you obey, you will be my friend and will have authority over affairs in my kingdom.”

While he was urging him in this way, he sent for the boy’s mother and had her brought in, so that, taking pity on herself after being bereaved of all these sons, she might persuade the one who remained to obey and live.
But when his mother encouraged him in the Hebrew language, as we are about to relate shortly,
He answered and said to the king and all his friends who were with him, “Release me.”
They were overjoyed at the boy’s promise and quickly released him.
But he ran beside one of the frying pans that were near him and said:
“Wicked tyrant, more wicked than all the wicked! Do not deny that you received blessings and kingship from God, yet you slaughter his servants and torture the champions of truth.
For these things God’s judgment awaits you: a fire fiercer than this one, burning forever. Tortures will never release you.

Are you not ashamed that, although you too are human, you cut out the tongues of human beings as though they were animals, and torture and burn them in this way? They can suffer just as you can and are made from the very same elements as you.”
“But they have fulfilled their duty of reverence for God.
“You, however, will groan bitterly because you killed his champions of truth without cause.
“And I too, who am about to die, say to you:
I will not turn away from the heroism of my brothers.
But I call upon the God of my fathers to be reconciled to our people.
But he will torment you both in this world and after your death.
After praying that these things would come upon the tyrant, he threw himself onto the frying pan and so gave up his spirit.
If, then, the seven boys scorned even the agonies of death, it is clear in every respect that reason rules over the passions.
For if they had submitted to their passions and eaten what was unclean, we would have said that they had been overcome by those passions.
But as it is, this did not happen. Instead, through reason directed toward God, they overcame their pains.
There is no denying the authority of reason, for they overcame both pains and passions.
How, then, can we fail to acknowledge that through understanding they gained victory over the passions, since they did not give way under the tortures of fire?
For just as towers built like barriers in front of harbors break the assault of the waves and allow those arriving from a voyage to find a peaceful harbor,
so too the wisdom of these young men, like seven towers, enclosed the harbor of reverence for God within fortifications and overcame the suffering caused by torture.
For they formed a splendid company in reverence for God and encouraged one another, saying:
“Brothers, let us die as brothers for the sake of the Law. Let us imitate the three young men in Assyria, who mastered their sufferings.”
Let us not shrink from showing our steadfastness.”
One would say, “Take courage, my brothers!” Another would say, “Let us endure bravely!”
Another reminded them, saying, “Remember where you come from, and at the hand of what father Isaac submitted to being slaughtered.”
Each of them, rejoicing and taking courage together, said, “Let us entrust our souls wholeheartedly to God, who gave us our souls, and let us give our bodies for the sake of keeping the Law.”
Let us not fear the one who appears to kill.

For the danger to the soul is great, since eternal punishment is appointed for those who transgress God's commandments. Let us therefore arm ourselves with the mastery over the passions possessed by the mind that fears God.
For when we die in this way, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob will receive us, and all our fathers will praise us.
As each one of them was torn away from his brothers, those who remained said to him, “Do not disgrace yourself, our brother. Do not betray these brothers of yours who have gone before.”

You are not unaware of the natural affection of humanity, which divine providence, wise in everything, has distributed through parents to their offspring and planted in them through their mother's womb.
In it the brothers completed equal periods of time, and in that very same womb they were formed. They grew from the very same blood, and from the same soul they sprang up and came to maturity.
They were born after equal periods of time, drank from the very same springs of milk, and were carried in the same lap. From these things, love for one another arose in their souls.
It flourished vigorously because of their shared upbringing and daily companionship with one another, their education in letters, and our distinctive training in the divine law.
Since brotherly affection is so dear, these seven brothers of ours were bound still more closely in love for one another.
For because they had been trained in the same law, instructed in the very same virtue, and brought up together in a righteous way of life, they loved one another all the more.
For the zeal for good things that was present in all of them further strengthened their love and harmony.
For along with the fear of God, this zeal itself made their brotherhood exceedingly dear to them.

But although nature, habit, and virtuous ways of life made their brotherly love flourish, those who remained accepted, for the sake of the truth, having to watch their brothers being tormented by torture.
And not only this: they also encouraged them to give themselves over to suffering, so that they would not only scorn the torments but also overcome the emotions of brotherly affection.
O thoughts that ruled more royally than kings and were freer than free men!
O the harmonious blending of the voices of the seven boys in defense of the truth!
Not one of the seven boys lost heart, nor did they fear death.
Instead, as though running along the road to immortality, they all hurried toward death through torture.

For just as hands and feet are moved together by the impulses of the soul, so those splendid youths, as though moved by an immortal soul, agreed with one another through their fear of God to die for it.
O holy company of seven harmonious brothers! For just as the seven days of creation revolve around the observances of the law,
so these young men also circled about, rejoicing in their company of seven and dispelling the fear of torture.
Now we shudder when we hear of the sufferings of those young men. But they not only actually saw them, and not only heard a sudden word of threat: even while they suffered, they were victorious.
They overcame the fierce pains of fire, than which nothing is harsher. Because the fire's power was fierce and swift, it quickly consumed their bodies.
Do not think it remarkable that the minds of those men endured amid torture, when even this woman's heart triumphed over emotions more powerful than these.
For the mother of these seven young men bore within herself the tortures inflicted on each one of them.
Consider how numerous are the tangled roots of love for children. For affection flows through all the [?].
Even animals without reason have toward their offspring a bond of love like that of human beings.
For even among birds, the one that peacefully enters a house beneath its roof fights for her chicks.
But the one that builds her nest and places her chicks on mountain peaks, on rocky crags, in the hollows of trees, and on their tops.
She prevents them from being caught, flying over them and circling around them. Her affection makes her suffer, and she calls to them with her voice and helps her young as much as she can.
But why is it necessary to demonstrate the love that animals without reason have for their young?

Likewise, bees, when they are building their honeycombs, stand guard and become fierce toward those who try to approach them. With their stings they strike those who approach their young as though with iron weapons, and they fight back to the death.
But love for her children did not shake the soul of the boys’ mother, which was like Abraham’s.
O mind that ruled over the sufferings of her children! O truth, whom a mother loved more than her children!
The mother, when two things were set before her eyes—love of torments and a full lifetime for her seven sons, according to the tyrant’s promise—[?].
She chose for herself love of truth, which gives eternal life in God.

Oh, how shall I describe the different feelings involved in love for children? For a person’s likeness is wonderfully imprinted on the little faces of the children, and because of this, her feelings incline her toward affection.
For the weaker mothers’ souls are, and the more children they bear, the more deeply they love their children.
But the mother of the seven loved her sons more than all other mothers. Through seven pregnancies, love for them had been planted within her.
Because of the birth pains she had suffered for each one of them, she was compelled to feel affection for them.
Yet because of her fear of God, she scorned her children's earthly lives.
That is, because of their nobility and their obedience to the law, she had acquired an even greater affection for them.
For they were righteous, chaste, strong, and courageous. They loved one another and loved their mother. Indeed, they loved her so much that they obeyed her even to death, while keeping the law.
But although all these things were so, drawing the mother toward tender feelings through her love for her children, the various tortures could not change her resolve in the case of even one of them.
Instead, she encouraged each one of them individually, and all of them together, to die for the truth.
O radiant mind and love of these parents! O childbirth and upbringing full of love, and a mother’s affection that cannot be softened!
As she saw each one of them subjected to torture and burning, she remained unchanged for the sake of the truth.

She saw her sons’ flesh melting over the fire, their fingers and toes writhing on the ground, and the skin of their heads stripped away down to the flesh of their chins and draped over their heads like unfamiliar faces.
Oh, the bitter sufferings into which the mother had now entered, worse than when she lay in labor with them!
O woman, you alone were perfect in the fear of God!
Your firstborn did not change your resolve as his life departed from him, nor did the next, who looked at you tenderly from amid his tortures, nor the third, as he passed from life.
Yet as you looked into the eyes of each one of them, whose gaze was altered by suffering, and at their nostrils, which gave advance warning of death, you did not weep.

When you saw more of your sons’ flesh being cut off on top of the flesh already cut away, hands being severed after hands, scalps being stripped off after scalps, and dead bodies falling upon dead bodies, and when you saw the tyrant’s soldiers descending upon your sons like a whirlwind, you shed no tears.
The melody of the Sirens and the sound of swans do not draw their listeners to delight in hearing as much as the voices of the sons crying out from their tortures.
What kinds, and how many! But the mother, while her sons were being afflicted and tormented on wheels and with branding irons—
She was enduring torments. But amid these sufferings, her God-fearing mind overcame her affections and gave her strength to despise the passing love of children.
Although she saw the destruction of her seven sons and the many different forms of their torture, the victorious mother uprooted that love and cast it away because of her faith in God.
For it was as though she saw, in a council chamber, the evil counselors of her own soul: nature, childbirth, love for children, and the tortures of her children.
The mother considered two verdicts: one of death and one of life.
For her sons' sake, she did not choose what would keep her seven sons alive for a full span of time.
Instead, as a daughter of Abraham, she remembered her steadfastness in God.
O mother of the people, avenger of the dishonor done to the law, and champion of the truth! You won the victory in the struggle with your own affections.
O woman who surpassed men in endurance!
For just as Noah’s [?], in the flood that destroyed the whole world, kept creation safe within it and sustained it, so you bravely endured [?].

So too you, guardian of the law, were lashed on every side by a surge of sufferings. Fierce winds—the tortures of your sons—blew against you from every direction. You courageously endured the storms that came upon you for the sake of the truth.
If, then, an elderly woman, the mother of seven young men, endured the sight of her sons being tortured to death, it is clear that a mind filled with the fear of God rules over the passions.
I have therefore shown that not only men overcame the passions, but a woman too scorned terrible tortures.

Daniel’s lions were not so savage, nor was Mishael’s furnace, blazing with fierce fire, so intense as the burning of her natural love for her children, as she watched her seven sons being killed in such different ways.
But through a mind governed by the fear of God, the mother quenched these feelings and others like them.
Consider this too: if she had been a woman weak in spirit, especially since she was also a mother, she would have mourned over them and said things like these:
“Oh, weak and utterly wretched woman that I am! I bore seven sons, yet I have not been a mother to a single one of them!
“Oh, seven pregnancies that came to nothing, births after ten months each that proved useless and fruitless, and pure nourishment with milk!
“In vain, children, I endured many labor pains for you, and the hard work of caring for you as you grew up.
“Some of you did not marry, while those who did married in vain. I do not see your children, nor do people call me blessed when I am called a mother of sons.
“Oh, a woman with many sons and fine sons, yet a widow! My sorrows alone have multiplied.
“Even when I die, I will not have one of my sons to bury me.” But the blessed mother who feared God did not utter even one of these laments.
She did not hold them back to keep them from dying, nor was she distressed when they died.

Instead, she had a mind like adamant, and she was again in labor to give birth to all her sons into immortality. She urged them all the more toward death for the sake of the truth, pleading with them and imploring them.
O mother who labored in old age for the sake of the truth! O elderly woman who defeated the tyrant through your endurance and proved yourself stronger than men in both deeds and words!
For when you were arrested with your sons, you stood watching Eleazar being tortured, and you said to your sons in the Hebrew language:
“My sons, mighty is the contest to which we have been called, to fight with resolute minds for the testimony of our people and for the law of our fathers.
“For it would be a disgrace if this old man endured sufferings for the fear of God, while you, who are young, shrank back from the truth.
“Remember that it was because of God that you came into the world and entered this life.
“Therefore you are obliged to endure every hardship for God’s sake.

“For its sake our father Abraham also eagerly prepared to sacrifice his son Isaac, the father of our people. For Isaac himself did not tremble when he saw his father’s hand holding the knife and descending upon him.
“Righteous Daniel fell among the lions, and Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were hurled into the furnace as though from a sling, and they endured for God’s sake.”
“You, then, who have the very same faith in God as they did, must not complain.
“For it is foolish, when you know what the fear of God is, not to stand firm in the face of torments.”
With these words the mother of the seven pleaded with each of her sons to die rather than transgress God’s commandment.
You should know that those who have died for God are alive to God, just as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the patriarchs are.
Some of the soldiers also said that, when she too was about to be seized and put to death, she willingly threw herself into the fire so that no one would touch her body.
O mother, together with your seven sons you overthrew the tyrant’s violence, frustrated his schemes, and demonstrated the strength of your faith!
For you were like a roof, resting firmly on your sons as on pillars, and without fire [?] you endured the shaking caused by tortures.
So take courage now, O glorious mother, for the hope arising from your endurance has been confirmed for you with God.

The moon in heaven is not as splendid as you are honored before God. You took your seven victorious sons by the hand and enlightened them so that they would come to the truth, and you are with them in heaven.
For your sons were descended from our father Abraham.
If it were easy for us to paint the story of your love of truth on something, those who looked at it would shudder to see a mother of seven sons enduring various tortures for the sake of the truth.
Indeed, in praise of your death, it would be fitting to write these words on your tomb, to speak to the people and remind them.
For here the aged priest, the elderly woman, and her seven sons contend nobly against the tyrant who wanted to overthrow the ordinances of the law and the way of life of the Hebrews.
They avenged the dishonor done to the law and the people, looking to God, and endured tortures to the point of death.”
For the contest they undertook was truly a contest for God’s sake.
For virtue had then established the contest, choosing victory for itself through endurance and granting incorruptibility in undying life.
Eleazar was the first to enter the contest. Afterward, the seven young men and their mother fought.
The tyrant was the opponent, and the world was the spectator.
But the fear of God was victorious, crowning its athletes.
Who was not astonished at these athletes of divine virtue? Who did not marvel?
The tyrant himself and all his counselors were astonished at their endurance.
Because of it, they stand beside the divine throne and dwell in a place full of rest and blessings.
For Moses also said, “All the holy ones are under their hands.”
Thus they were made holy and were honored for God's sake—not only with this honor, but also because through them our people defeated their enemies.
The tyrant received punishment, and our land was purified.
For the blood of these blessed people was poured out for the sins of the people, and their death was an atonement. God's providence rescued Israel, which was being afflicted.

For the tyrant Antiochus, delighted by their courageous virtue and their perseverance under affliction, proclaimed to his soldiers that they should imitate their endurance. He encouraged them, following this example,
to be vigorous and courageous as infantry and cavalry, so that they would conquer cities by siege. In this way he defeated and devastated all his enemies.
O children descended from Abraham's own body, you children of Israel, obey this law and honor it in every way,
as people who acknowledge that the mind devoted to the fear of God has authority over the passions. It rules not only over the passions within, but also over pains inflicted from outside.
For because those victorious ones surrendered their bodies to affliction for the truth, not only did people marvel at them, but they were also counted worthy of a divine portion.
Because of them our people lived in peace, renewed the ordinances of their laws in their own land, and defeated their enemies.

But the tyrant Antiochus received punishment even here on earth, and now that he is dead he is in torment. For he could not compel the people of Jerusalem by any means to do anything that departed from the custom of their ancestors.
Then he withdrew from the people of Jerusalem and marched with his army against the Persians. The mother used to speak these fitting words to her sons:
“I was a pure virgin and did not leave my father's house, but guarded my virginity against every injury.
No ravisher approached me in the city, as in the wilderness, nor did a seducer, harmful to the sight, injure my virginity. In my youth I lived with a husband.

After you were born to him and had grown up, your father died. Blessed is he! For although he was a man who desired a life in which he would have many children, he did not have to lament the loss of his sons.
He was the one who taught you the Law and the Prophets while he was still with you.
He used to teach you about Abel, who was killed by Cain, and read to you about Isaac's whole burnt offering and Joseph in prison.
He used to tell you about Phinehas the zealous, and recount to you the story of Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael in the fire.
He also used to praise Daniel in the lions' den.
He used to remind you of the book of Isaiah, who said, ‘Even if you pass through fire, the flame will not burn you.’
He used to sing to you the words of David, the writer of songs, who said, ‘Many are the troubles of the righteous.’
He used to tell you a proverb from Solomon: ‘It is a tree of life to those who do his will.’
He used to affirm the words of Ezekiel, who said, ‘These dry bones will live.’
Nor did he forget the song that Moses taught, teaching you its words: ‘I put to death, and I give life.’”
These are our life and the length of our days.”

O that bitter day, and yet not bitter, when the king of the Greeks extinguished fire with fire, bringing the blessed ones to fiercely heated cauldrons and a hot [?], with spits and instruments of torture that he had prepared for the seven sons of Abraham's daughter!
He pierced the pupils of their eyes, cut out their tongues, and killed them with bitter tortures.
For these things divine judgment tormented him, and it will torment him again—the tyrant who became like a destructive demon.
But Abraham's sons, together with their victorious mother, dwell in purity of soul and in the immortality they received from God.
To him be glory and honor, now and forever and ever. Amen. The discourse on the Maccabees and their mother is finished.
